main.title: Chase H.Q.
main.summary: Chase H.Q. is a 1988 vehicular combat video game developed and published by Taito for arcades.

cards.text: Chase H.Q. is a 1988 vehicular combat video game developed and published by Taito for arcades. The player assumes the role of a police officer named Tony Gibson, member of the "Chase Special Investigation Department". Along with his partner, Raymond Broady, he must stop fleeing criminals in high-speed pursuits in a black Porsche 928.

Chase H.Q. was ported to many home computers by Ocean Software in 1989, including versions for the ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, MSX, Amiga and Atari ST. Taito produced versions for the Family Computer (1989), Game Boy (1990), Master System (1990), TurboGrafx-16 (1990), Game Gear (1991), and Saturn (1996). It was released for PlayStation 2 in Japan in 2007 as part of Taito Memories II Volume 2.

The game was a commercial success, becoming Japan's highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1989 while also becoming a hit overseas for arcades and home systems. The game was also well received by critics. It was followed by three arcade-based sequels: Special Criminal Investigation (1989), Super Chase H.Q. (1992) and Chase H.Q. 2 (2007). Two spin-offs were also released: Crime City (1989) and Quiz H.Q. (1990).

main.title: The Guardian Legend
main.subtitle: A world approaching Earth
main.summary: The Guardian Legend is Compile’s unusual combination of exploration and vertically scrolling shooting for the NES. Its heroine, the Guardian, must stop the alien world Naju before it reaches Earth. On the surface she moves in humanoid form through an interconnected labyrinth; inside its corridors she becomes a spacecraft. The objective links both forms: find and deactivate ten safety devices to trigger Naju’s destruction. Instead of placing two unrelated games beside each other, Compile makes exploration supply the routes and equipment for the next flight.

cards.heading: A world approaching Earth
cards.text: The Guardian Legend is Compile’s unusual combination of exploration and vertically scrolling shooting for the NES. Its heroine, the Guardian, must stop the alien world Naju before it reaches Earth. On the surface she moves in humanoid form through an interconnected labyrinth; inside its corridors she becomes a spacecraft. The objective links both forms: find and deactivate ten safety devices to trigger Naju’s destruction. Instead of placing two unrelated games beside each other, Compile makes exploration supply the routes and equipment for the next flight.

cards.heading: Chips for firepower and supplies
cards.text: The Guardian carries a rapid-fire weapon with unlimited ammunition and a selection of more powerful secondary weapons. Those extra attacks consume power chips, which also serve as money in Naju’s shops. Firing freely can therefore spend a resource that might have bought an improvement later. New weapons and upgrades are found through exploration or awarded after bosses. The choice of what to use in a corridor belongs to a longer preparation, because the next area is connected to what the Guardian has already discovered.

cards.heading: Two views of the same journey
cards.text: The surface gives the player room to decide where to investigate, while the shooting corridors turn that preparation into a concentrated test of movement and aim. A map that seems large and uncertain becomes a stream of immediate threats once the Guardian changes form. Returning to the labyrinth then restores the question of direction. This alternation is the game’s defining achievement: the pace can change sharply without abandoning the journey, since both halves concern the same hostile world and the equipment needed to survive it.

main.title: Dragon Quest III
main.summary: Dragon Quest III: The Seeds of Salvation, titled Dragon Warrior III when initially localized to North America, is a 1988 role-playing video game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix.

cards.text: Dragon Quest III is Chunsoft and Enix's 1988 role-playing game, first released for Japan's Famicom and later known in North America as Dragon Warrior III. It became a repeatedly revisited part of the series, returning in enhanced versions for Super Famicom and Game Boy Color and later on mobile devices. The English subtitle The Seeds of Salvation accompanied the international mobile release in 2014. A further recreation, Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake, brought the game to Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows and Xbox Series in November 2024.

The first three Dragon Quest games are all part of the same overarching story, collectively known as the "Erdrick trilogy". However, Dragon Quest III is a distant prequel to the previous two games, taking place long before the events of the first game. It follows the Hero destined to earn the title of "Erdrick," who must take up his father's quest to save the world from the villainous archfiend Baramos. Gathering a group of companions into a party, the Hero must travel the world, stopping at various towns and locations, and gather the strength needed to take the archfiend down.

main.title: Captain Tsubasa
main.summary: Tecmo's 1988 Famicom football role-playing game adapts the Captain Tsubasa manga; a substantially relocalised version followed overseas as Tecmo Cup Soccer Game in 1992.

cards.text: Captain Tsubasa is Tecmo's football role-playing game for the Famicom, released in Japan in 1988. Based on the manga series, it gives players skill levels and organises much of its action through text commands. These elements combine football matches with a role-playing approach to the team.

The 1992 Western adaptation became Tecmo Cup Soccer Game, also called Tecmo Cup Football Game in Europe. It changed the main character, introduction and player designs for its overseas audience. The original Captain Tsubasa and this later adaptation therefore share their basic approach to football while presenting different casts.

main.title: Arc System Works
main.subtitle: Arc System Works Turns Drawn Animation into a Fighting System
main.summary: Arc System Works was legally established on May 12, 1988.

cards.heading: Arc System Works Turns Drawn Animation into a Fighting System
cards.text: Arc System Works was established on May 12, 1988. Beginning with programming for other companies, it later became associated with Guilty Gear and BlazBlue. Their fighting systems combine distinctive characters, animation and music. For its transition to 3D, the studio developed techniques that let models retain the appearance of drawn animation.

cards.heading: Before the Brand, the Craft
cards.text: Contract development gave Arc System Works experience across hardware and genres before its own properties became widely recognised. Programming, tools and porting work formed an important part of those early years. Developing original games brought that production experience together with characters and systems of the studio's own.

cards.heading: Guilty Gear Chooses Excess
cards.text: Guilty Gear pairs exaggerated characters and hard-rock music with fighting built around movement, pressure and detailed system knowledge. Poses, effects and sound give quick feedback when attacks connect or a defence opens. The presentation must remain readable during rapid exchanges so players can respond to what the opponent is doing.

cards.heading: BlazBlue Organizes Complexity
cards.text: BlazBlue's Drive system assigns one button a different central function for each fighter. Choosing a character changes more than the available combos: the player must learn that character's particular rule and how it works against the rest of the roster. Distinct animation and clear feedback help communicate these differences during a match.

main.title: Kenseiden
main.subtitle: A samurai crosses the provinces
main.summary: Kenseiden is Sega's sword-fighting platform adventure, first released for Master System in Japan on 2 June 1988.

cards.heading: A samurai crosses the provinces
cards.text: Kenseiden is Sega's sword-fighting platform adventure, first released for Master System in Japan on 2 June 1988. The samurai Hayato travels through sixteenth-century provinces to recover five scrolls and a sacred sword from hostile warlocks and spirits. Side-view stages provide the individual encounters, placing enemies and obstacles around his movements. The larger journey eventually allows the player to choose the order of provinces, giving the adventure a map to consider beyond the next screen. Its Japanese setting connects the swordplay, creatures and locations into a recognisable supernatural expedition.

cards.heading: Choosing where to travel next
cards.text: Hayato must judge the reach of his sword while moving through the stage's platforms and approaching enemies. Clearing one province contributes to the wider search, but later freedom to choose a destination changes how the journey is organised. Returning to earlier locations also becomes possible before the final stage. The player can therefore treat the map as a set of places to investigate rather than an unbroken line of levels, deciding which route to attempt as the remaining scrolls and the ultimate confrontation draw the expedition onwards.

cards.heading: A journey with another route
cards.text: The side-view action keeps each province immediate, while the map supplies a sense of travelling across a larger country. Distinctive enemies and still scenes reinforce that scale within the Master System's presentation. A South Korean version changed Hayato into a Hwarang warrior and altered the setting, showing how substantially regional presentation could reshape the same underlying game. The original's lasting identity comes from combining a samurai's direct sword attacks with the freedom to revisit provinces, making the task feel like a journey through places with their own dangers and purposes.

main.title: Blaster Master
main.subtitle: Blaster Master Changes Perspective to Change How Space Is Understood
main.summary: On June 17, 1988 Sunsoft released Chou-Wakusei Senki MetaFight in Japan, the basis for the Western version Blaster Master.

cards.heading: Blaster Master Changes Perspective to Change How Space Is Understood
cards.text: Sunsoft released Chou-Wakusei Senki MetaFight in Japan on June 17, 1988, before adapting it for the West as Blaster Master. The action game alternates side-view exploration in the SOPHIA vehicle with top-down sections on foot. Leaving the tank opens smaller entrances, and defeating bosses provides abilities that allow further travel through the connected world.

cards.heading: Two viewpoints across eight connected levels
cards.text: Blaster Master has two modes of gameplay that depend on the situation and location of the player: the first mode is where the player controls Jason; either on foot or piloting a tank named SOPHIA in a two–dimensional platform mode; the second mode is where the player controls Jason on foot in a top-down perspective. Gameplay in the top-down perspective consists of a series of labyrinths in which players navigate and defeat enemies along the way. Gameplay is non-linear, and players must return to earlier levels in order to advance to later levels in the game. The objective is to complete all eight levels and destroy the mutants and their bosses with various weaponry such as guns, grenades, and special weapons.

cards.heading: SOPHIA’s cannon and limited special weapons
cards.text: While Jason is inside SOPHIA in the 2D platforming mode, the player can attack the mutants with the main cannon (which can shoot up, left, and right determined by the orientation of the tank) or with one of three special weapons. Special weapons have limited ammunition which must be collected from exploring the game. They include the following: homing missiles that, when fired, shoot 1 missile at each enemy on screen up to 4; "Thunder Break", which fires a high-damage lightning bolt downward; and "Multi Warhead Missiles", which simultaneously fires a set of three missiles at enemies in front of and diagonally up and down. Players select their special weapon and monitor the amounts of each special weapon left by accessing the Menu Screen by pressing the Start button.

cards.heading: Leaving the tank to earn new abilities
cards.text: The player switches between the 2D platforming mode and the top-down perspective by leaving the tank and entering small doorways located throughout the game. While in the top-down perspective, players can move Jason in any direction and destroy mutants with a gun or with hand grenades. In this mode, players upgrade the gun by collecting gun capsules, but the gun degrades by one point if Jason receives damage from mutants or hazardous objects. Here players obtain additional vehicle functions by destroying bosses; these functions include weapon upgrades as well as abilities to swim freely underwater, drive on walls and ceilings, and hover above the ground.

main.title: Nintendo Power
main.summary: Nintendo Fun Club News preceded Nintendo Power as a newsletter sent to club members for free. In mid-1988 it was discontinued after seven issues in favor of Nintendo Power. The new magazine was founded by Nintendo of America marketing manager Gail Tilden in 1988. The first issue, dated July/August 1988, spotlights the NES game Super Mario Bros. 2. Of this issue, 3.6 million copies were published, with every member of the Nintendo Fun Club receiving a free copy.

cards.heading: From the Fun Club to a magazine
cards.text: Nintendo Fun Club News preceded Nintendo Power as a newsletter sent to club members for free. In mid-1988 it was discontinued after seven issues in favor of Nintendo Power. The new magazine was founded by Nintendo of America marketing manager Gail Tilden in 1988. The first issue, dated July/August 1988, spotlights the NES game Super Mario Bros. 2. Of this issue, 3.6 million copies were published, with every member of the Nintendo Fun Club receiving a free copy.

cards.heading: Twenty-four years of Nintendo news
cards.text: Nintendo Power was a video game news and strategy magazine from Nintendo of America, first published in July/August 1988 as Nintendo's official print magazine for North America. The magazine's publication was initially done monthly by Nintendo of America, then independently, and in December 2007 contracted to Future US, the American subsidiary of British publisher Future plc. Its 24-year production run is one of the longest of all video game magazines in the United States and Canada.

cards.heading: Strategy between the covers
cards.text: From the beginning, Nintendo Power focuses heavily on providing game strategy, reviews, and previews of upcoming games. In mid-1998, Nintendo Power first allowed outside advertising in the magazine, formerly reserved for Nintendo-based products only. In its early years, ads only appeared in the first and last few pages of the magazine, leaving no ads to break up the magazine's editorial content.

cards.heading: The final printed issue
cards.text: On August 21, 2012, Nintendo announced that it would not be renewing its licensing agreement with Future Publishing, and that Nintendo Power would cease publication in December. The final issue, volume 285, was released on December 11, 2012.

cards.heading: A new life as a podcast
cards.text: On December 20, 2017, a podcast version of Nintendo Power was launched, which ran until 2023. It was hosted by Chris Slate, the former editor-in-chief of the magazine.

main.title: Capcom Bowling
main.summary: Capcom Bowling is a top down bowling sports simulation game developed by Incredible Technologies (under the brand name Strata) and released by Capcom to arcades in 1988.

cards.text: Capcom Bowling is a top-down bowling game developed by Incredible Technologies under its Strata name and released by Capcom in arcades in 1988. Up to four players take turns in a game. A trackball controls the direction and power of the delivery, while two buttons add left or right spin. Certain shots trigger comic animations.

The game was released in both an upright cabinet and a cocktail version. Most of the upright cabinets are conversion kits for existing cabinets although a limited number of dedicated cabinets were produced. These cabinets featured a birch plywood finish to mimic a bowling lane, a larger marbled trackball and painted side art. The Japanese version featured a different cabinet.

An alternate version, Coors Light Bowling, was released the following year. This version features endorsement from the beer Coors Light. The title screen is completely different on this version and some of the animations were changed to add Coors Light references.

main.title: Famicom Wars
main.subtitle: Famicom Wars Makes Strategy Readable One Tile at a Time
main.summary: On August 12, 1988 Nintendo released Famicom Wars in Japan.

cards.heading: Famicom Wars Makes Strategy Readable One Tile at a Time
cards.text: Nintendo released Famicom Wars in Japan on August 12, 1988. Its turn-based battles place infantry, tanks and other units on a grid alongside cities, ports and airports. Capturing territory increases the resources available for production and supports existing troops. Players must decide how to divide each turn between gaining ground, protecting units and preparing reinforcements.

cards.heading: Red Star and Blue Moon take turns
cards.text: Players take control of one of two warring nations, Red Star and Blue Moon, as they seek to establish turn-based dominance over each other. After selecting which stage to start the game and setting which, if either, player will be controlled by a person, the Red Star army is given the first turn.

cards.heading: Factories build units and captured cities support them
cards.text: During each turn, the player is given a certain amount of funds which can be used to build units in factories, seaports, and airports under their command; additional funds are earned by conquering cities near their headquarters. Each unit has their own speciality and unique abilities, with ten land units (including two foot soldier units), four air units, and two sea units. Some units have heavier firepower than others, while others provide support to allies. Only foot soldier units are capable of conquering cities, which can then be used to repair or refuel damaged units. There are 15 maps available at the start of the game, with two secret ending maps dependent on which nation the player fights for when playing against the computer.

cards.heading: Visible battles make the strategy easier to follow
cards.text: On release, Famicom Tsūshin four reviewers all complimented Famicom Wars. They all found it actively distinguishing itself from other simulation games which they described as dull or difficult to understand with information portrayed as numeric data. Two reviewers complimented the graphics and animation, with one saying the battle animations are realistic which will get the player more into the action. The 1989 "All Soft Catalog" issue of Famicom Tsūshin included Famicom Wars in its list of the best games of all time, giving it the Best Simulation and Best Commercial awards.
